extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science and journalism; newspaper editors and informed citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for the press' role in a democracy: how newspapers should gather and present information about the 'invisible environment', the civil liberties that protect that role, economic constraints on production, and institutional/audit mechanisms to render public life knowable and accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberties (freedom of expression and press)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maintenance of civil liberties (freedom of speech and of the press) is of fundamental importance; when these liberties are in jeopardy, the human spirit and the capacity for civilized recovery are endangered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend and maintain civil liberties even in wartime except where absolutely necessary; they are a basic precondition for independent journalism but do not by themselves guarantee accurate public opinion about complex matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free and truthful press
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should be 'free' and 'truthful' and present a true picture of the outer world in which readers are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ethical expectation is widespread and powerful — readers treat newspapers like moral institutions (comparable to schools or churches) — but truthfulness alone is hard to achieve for distant/complex issues without institutional support, expertise, and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as the chief means of contact with the invisible environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are the primary means by which citizens learn about the distant and complex realities (the 'invisible environment') that shape public life and government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these matters are not self-evident, the press must perform the technical task of making them intelligible; political science and democratic theory historically underemphasized this role of news-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketplace-of-ideas limitation for complex matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The classic doctrine that free competition of opinions will produce truth is inadequate when dealing with distant or complex affairs; truth in such domains is not self-evident and will not emerge simply from debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on free expression and open argument is insufficient for producing accurate public opinion about matters that require technical reporting, sustained investigation, or specialized knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and costly nature of news-gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: The machinery for assembling information about modern public life is technical and expensive; reporting complex realities requires institutional capacity and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that accurate reporting demands investment (expert reporters, bureaus, investigations). Expecting spontaneous, low-cost distribution of such information is unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic model and consumer expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers typically expect newspapers to provide information at minimal cost (often treating news as virtually free), and the casual relationship between readers and the press is an anomaly of modern civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because much news is sold below cost and readers will switch or stop paying easily, the press faces commercial pressures that affect editorial independence and quality; editors must maintain readership continuously ('re-elected every day').

rubrics_metrics.name: Press judged by communal ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethically the press is judged as if it were a public moral institution (like a school or church) rather than a purely commercial enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shapes public expectations: newspapers are expected to serve the public good and be truthful even when those services are costly or unprofitable; policymakers and practitioners should be aware of this normative frame when designing funding and regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for institutions and public education to render the invisible environment visible
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of institutions and education that reliably report the environment, common interests largely elude public opinion and management of public affairs falls to a specialized class acting on non-public information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build institutions (news organizations, public information services) and civic education so citizens can grasp complex public realities; otherwise expert or specialized administrators will exercise power without effective democratic oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of living and objective audits as criteria for government
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic accountability should rely on objective standards of living (health, housing, education, etc.) and on audits that plainly record the acts and measure the results of public officials and industrial directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop precise, public standards and audit mechanisms so that the exercise of power can be assessed by outcomes rather than only by source-of-power or rhetorical expression; this increases real public control over officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press responsibility to present the relevant picture of public life
rubrics_metrics.description: The press has the responsibility to present a true and usable picture of those parts of the outer world that matter to citizens' interests and to government decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and newsrooms should prioritize and invest in coverage that illuminates the invisible environment and helps citizens form informed judgments; recognize practical limits (attention, resources) and design beats/institutions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that self-centered opinion is insufficient for good government
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-centered opinions, formed from narrow direct experience, are not sufficient for good government in a complex society; news institutions must compensate for this limitation by informing and educating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news output by its capacity to broaden public understanding beyond parochial perspectives and to enable conception of common interests; prioritize explanatory/reporting work that translates specialist knowledge into publicly accessible forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and political vulnerability of news to contestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because newspapers influence taxation, wages, prices and other material interests, and because readers seldom pay much, news organizations are economically and politically vulnerable to passionate contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional protections and funding approaches (diversified revenue, public support mechanisms, strong editorial independence norms) to reduce capture by partisan or commercial pressures and to sustain investigative and explanatory journalism.
